title: Operation Uranus begins
pull: 3,500 guns open up in the fog

facts.text: At 07:20 Moscow time on 19 November 1942, Soviet gunners on the Don northwest of Stalingrad received the code word "Siren". Ten minutes later about 3,500 guns and mortars opened fire.
Fog and snow hid the targets, so the gunners could not correct their aim, but they had ranged in days before and the fire stayed accurate.
At 08:50 the Southwestern Front's 5th Tank and 21st Armies attacked the Romanian Third Army from the Serafimovich bridgehead and near Kletskaya, with the Don Front's 65th Army alongside.
The Romanians had no antitank guns heavier than 47 mm. Their line broke by noon, and Soviet tank corps drove through the gaps that afternoon.
At 22:00 Army Group B ordered all German attacks inside Stalingrad stopped at once and pulled panzer divisions out of the city to face the threat.
On 20 November the Stalingrad Front struck from south of the city, after fog had delayed the start for several hours.
On 23 November the two pincers met near Sovetsky, just east of Kalach on the Don. The German Sixth Army and part of the Fourth Panzer Army were trapped.
Estimates of the Axis troops inside the ring run from about 250,000 to 300,000. Soviet commanders at first believed they had caught only 85,000 to 90,000.
The plan had been prepared in secret. Between 1 and 19 November, boats of the Volga Flotilla carried 160,000 troops and 430 tanks across the river to the Stalingrad Front, moving at night.
Hitler ordered the Sixth Army to hold where it stood and be supplied by air. It surrendered at the start of February 1943.

photoNote: Soviet tank crews refuel during the winter advance, 1942 to 1943, with T-34s behind them in a snowy village. Unknown Soviet photographer, credited to the Ukrainian Central State Archive (scanned from S. Walsh, Stalingrad, the Infernal Cauldron, 2000). Commons tags PD-Russia-1996 and PD-Ukraine. Not dated to 19 November or captioned to Uranus itself; it is the Stalingrad winter offensive period, so caption it as winter 1942 to 1943. Portrait frame, 960 x 1563 (Commons original 974 x 1586); for the card crop the upper half with the T-34 and the two men. No PD photo of the opening barrage or the Kalach link up was found (the well known link up photos are RIA Novosti, CC BY SA).
photoCredit: Soviet tank crews refuel during the winter offensive near Stalingrad, 1942 to 1943. Unknown Soviet photographer, public domain.

declassified.fact: The Don bridge at Kalach fell by a trick. At 06:15 on 22 November a Soviet column led by two captured German tanks and a reconnaissance car drove onto it with their lights on, so the guards took them for their own, then opened fire.

film.record: The Battle of Russia (1943, U.S. War Department, Why We Fight 5), 111-OF-5 reel 10 (NARA 36071)
film.shot_notes: Reel 10 of 10, 10 min 36 s, narration and score throughout, so the clip runs silent. The Stalingrad counteroffensive: 01:18 to 01:30 Soviet cavalry crossing the snow, 01:32 to 01:48 long columns of infantry marching, 01:52 Rokossovsky (title card, avoid), 02:00 to 02:12 animated map of the pincers (avoid), 02:14 to 02:30 infantry charging across the snow, 02:32 an embrace that may be the staged link up (the Film Library calls the Stalingrad film's link up embrace staged; leave it out). 04:40 to 05:12 tanks and smoke belong to Operation Ring, January 1943 (not this card). Open on the cavalry or the charge. Soviet newsreel inside a U.S. film; not German film.
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. War Department, Why We Fight series); the Soviet footage inside it is Soviet newsreel used in a U.S. government film (the Videos doc's route to the Eastern Front). NARA use status 'Restricted, Possibly'.
film.date_note: Soviet film of the winter counteroffensive at Stalingrad, from the U.S. Army's The Battle of Russia; shots are not dated to 19 November, so the caption should say Soviet film of the Stalingrad counteroffensive, November 1942. A sharper alternative with the real Uranus barrage is the Soviet film Stalingrad (1943) in Source Film, STG 00:41:46 to 00:44:48 (needs Brian).
